## Home — https://xiao-yun-hu.github.io/marketing-simulation-lab/

Marketing Simulation Lab builds synthetic consumer behavior simulation for e-commerce and product teams: we use calibrated language-model populations to diagnose buying friction, compare page and message changes, and prioritize which experiments are worth running in the real world. This is early-stage research and product development, not a replacement for human research — simulation proposes, reality decides.

The method: (1) Discover — connect product pages with reviews, questions and available signals to surface evidence-linked hypotheses about what holds shoppers back. (2) Simulate — change one decision variable and compare how a synthetic consumer population interprets information and weighs trade-offs. (3) Validate — take promising changes into controlled real-world tests and compare simulated rankings against observed outcomes.

Founders: Rachel Hu, Co-Founder/CEO — eight years in data science and business analytics, focused on turning complex behavior into actionable business decisions. Dr. Tong Liu, Co-Founder/CTO — Marketing PhD specializing in consumer behavior, bringing behavioral research into the design of simulation systems.

Two live product experiences: Digital World (https://xiao-yun-hu.github.io/marketing-simulation-lab/a/) and Decision Intelligence Scanner (https://xiao-yun-hu.github.io/marketing-simulation-lab/scanner/), run side by side as an ongoing design experiment. A random-entry link at /go/ assigns new visitors to one of the two.

---

## What Are Synthetic Consumers? — https://xiao-yun-hu.github.io/marketing-simulation-lab/synthetic-consumers/

Synthetic consumers are simulated shoppers generated by large language models, used to produce and pressure-test hypotheses about buying behavior before — not instead of — real consumer research. They respond to product pages, offers or messaging the way a modeled population might, so a team can explore many "what if" variations quickly, then validate the strongest ones with real people.

Comparison:
- Marketing persona: a static, human-authored archetype, used for team alignment and messaging direction.
- Synthetic respondent: an LLM prompted to answer a survey instrument as if it were a population member; best for early-stage survey piloting.
- Synthetic consumer (Marketing Simulation Lab's usage): a simulated shopper that interacts with an actual product page, offer or decision scenario, not just a survey question; best for diagnosing friction in a specific page or flow before a real A/B test.
- Digital twin: a model of one specific, identifiable real customer, built from that person's real data; best for personalization and account-level forecasting.

When it applies: triaging many candidate changes down to a short list worth real-world testing; diagnosing why a page might be losing shoppers; exploring low-traffic scenarios a real A/B test would take too long to reach significance on.
When it doesn't: as the sole basis for a final launch decision; for populations the underlying model represents poorly; as a substitute for disclosure that a result is simulated, not measured.

---

## Consumer Behavior Simulation: Method & Use Cases — https://xiao-yun-hu.github.io/marketing-simulation-lab/consumer-behavior-simulation/

Consumer behavior simulation is a three-step pipeline — discover, simulate, validate — that uses a modeled population of synthetic consumers to test hypotheses about buying friction before committing real traffic to a real A/B test. It's built to triage ideas quickly, not to replace the real test that ultimately confirms them.

1. Discover: connect the commerce artifact being evaluated with available customer-voice signals — reviews, support questions, known objections.
2. Simulate: change one decision variable at a time and run a simulated consumer population against both versions.
3. Validate: take the highest-signal changes into a controlled real-world experiment and compare the simulated ranking against the real outcome.

E-commerce use cases: landing and product pages (what information is missing that's stopping the purchase — active, current focus); positioning and offers (which framing changes how shoppers evaluate a product — active research direction); agent commerce (how people and AI shopping agents clarify needs and compare trade-offs differently — roadmap direction, not yet commercially available).

Simulation is good at generating and ranking candidate hypotheses quickly and surfacing friction a team hadn't considered. It is not good at producing a number that should be published as a measured conversion lift, and should not be the only evidence behind a final launch decision.

---

## Research, Calibration & Known Limits — https://xiao-yun-hu.github.io/marketing-simulation-lab/research/

Internal research notes (2026, not independently audited, treat as directional):
- Ad copy credibility (two-sided messaging): human survey +0.54 points vs. simulation +0.30 points on a 1–7 credibility scale. Direction aligned; effect sizes did not. Directional comparison only.
- Product information completeness: simulated resolution of shopper questions rose 25–50 percentage points after clearer after-sales summaries, across two product contexts. Internal simulation outcome, not a measured real-world conversion lift.

External published research cited on this page:
- Kaiser, Kaiser, Schallner, Manewitsch & Rau, "Leaving Insight to Digital Twins? Promise, Progress and Limits of Synthetic Respondents," NIM Marketing Intelligence Review 18(1), 2026 (https://nim.org/en/publications/detail/leaving-insight-to-digital-twins) — GPT-4o digital-twin responses tracked real, quota-matched consumers reasonably well in aggregate, but were measurably weaker at predicting individual responses.
- Argyle et al., "Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples," Political Analysis 31(3), 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06899) — an LLM conditioned on real respondents' sociodemographic backstories reproduced fine-grained demographic response patterns ("algorithmic fidelity"), while the paper itself notes this comes with "not one bias, but many."
- Santurkar et al., "Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?" ICML 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.17548) — found substantial misalignment between LM-reflected opinions and roughly 60 real US demographic groups, persisting even after prompting the model to adopt a group's perspective.
- Park et al., "Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior," UIST 2023 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442) — LLM agents with observation/planning/reflection produced believable simulated social behavior in a sandbox; an architecture reference, not a market-research validation study.
- Aggarwal et al., "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization," KDD 2024 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) — proposes metrics for a source's visibility inside AI-generated answers (not a search-ranking position); found that adding citations and quotations could increase that visibility in their benchmark, with results varying by domain. Not a ranking guarantee.

Where simulation should not be trusted alone: final launch or budget decisions; small, niche or culturally specific populations the underlying model may represent poorly; any claim intended for external publication as a measured result.
